title: Swim in Rising Water
description: Brute force to optimized: binary search with reachability checks versus a Dijkstra-like priority search tracking a running maximum.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an n by n grid where grid[i][j] is the elevation at that cell, and water level rises by 1 unit every time step (a cell becomes passable once the water level is at least its elevation), return the minimum time until it is possible to swim from the top-left to the bottom-right corner.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","grid of elevations"],["Output","Minimum time (water level) at which top-left connects to bottom-right"],["Key Insight","The \"cost\" of a path is the MAXIMUM elevation along it, not a sum; this is a minimax path problem, solvable with a Dijkstra-like priority search"],["Constraints","Up to 50 by 50 grid"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Minimize the MAXIMUM value along a path\" (not a sum)","A minimax path problem, solvable via a Dijkstra-like greedy priority search (always expanding the lowest-elevation reachable cell next), or via binary search combined with BFS/DFS reachability checks"]]}

blocks.text: Unlike standard shortest-path problems that MINIMIZE A SUM of edge weights, this problem minimizes the MAXIMUM elevation encountered along any path from start to destination. The answer is the smallest possible value of "the highest elevation you must pass through" across all possible paths, since you only need the water level to reach that highest point, not every point along the way individually.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding a Hiking Route That Minimizes the Highest Peak You Must Cross
blocks.text: Picture planning a hiking route between two points across varied terrain, where the difficulty of a route is determined by its SINGLE HIGHEST peak, not the sum of all elevations along the way. The best route minimizes that one highest peak, even if it means a longer overall path.

blocks.caption: The path cost is the MAXIMUM elevation along it, not a sum, a minimax path problem

blocks.text: Result: 3 (at time 3, all cells are passable, and a path exists; waiting less would leave some required cell impassable).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A path's "cost" is the MAXIMUM elevation of any cell along it, not the sum of elevations, since water level only needs to reach that single highest point for the whole path to become passable.

Observation 2: This is analogous to Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm, but instead of summing edge weights, the "distance" to a cell is defined as the maximum elevation seen so far along the best path reaching it.

Observation 3: Using a priority structure (always expanding the currently lowest "maximum elevation so far" reachable cell next) correctly and greedily finds the true minimum possible "highest point" needed to reach every cell, analogous to Dijkstra's greedy nearest-node selection.

Observation 4: The moment the bottom-right cell is popped from this priority structure, the accumulated maximum elevation along that path is the answer, guaranteed minimal by the same greedy argument that makes Dijkstra's algorithm correct.
This leads to a Dijkstra-like priority search, tracking the maximum elevation seen so far along each path instead of a summed distance.
Binary search on the candidate answer time T; for each T, check via BFS/DFS whether top-left can reach bottom-right using only cells with elevation at most T.
Why the code is written this way

items: Binary searching the answer and checking reachability per candidate directly implements a "guess and verify" strategy.
This requires a fresh reachability check (BFS/DFS) for every candidate T tried during the binary search; a single Dijkstra-like priority search finds the exact answer directly in one pass.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared times log(n squared)), a reachability check per binary search step.
Space: O(n squared) per check.
Limitation: a single Dijkstra-like priority search finds the exact minimal "highest point" needed directly, without repeated reachability checks across a binary search.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Use a priority structure (conceptually a min-heap) seeded with the starting cell, keyed by its own elevation. Repeatedly extract the cell with the SMALLEST key; track a running "answer" as the maximum key extracted so far. If the extracted cell is the destination, return the running answer immediately. Otherwise, for each unvisited neighbor, mark it visited and insert it into the priority structure, keyed by ITS OWN elevation (not accumulated with the path so far, since only the SINGLE highest point along the path matters, not a sum).
Use a Dijkstra-like priority search, tracking the maximum elevation seen so far, expanding the lowest-elevation reachable cell each step.

codes.python:
import heapq

def swim_in_water(grid):
    n = len(grid)
    visited = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
    heap = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]
    visited[0][0] = True
    ans = 0
    while heap:
        t, r, c = heapq.heappop(heap)                        # smallest elevation reachable next
        ans = max(ans, t)                                       # track the max seen so far
        if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1:
            return ans
        for dr, dc in [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)]:
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and not visited[nr][nc]:
                visited[nr][nc] = True
                heapq.heappush(heap, (grid[nr][nc], nr, nc))       # keyed by its OWN elevation
    return ans

blocks.text: Always expanding the currently lowest-elevation reachable cell next (a Dijkstra-like greedy strategy) guarantees that once a cell is extracted, the running "answer" tracked so far is already the TRUE minimal maximum elevation needed to reach it, since any alternative path would have to pass through some cell with elevation at least as high before reaching it; tracking each candidate cell by its OWN elevation (not a summed cost) correctly reflects that only the single highest point along a path matters, and the moment the destination is extracted, the running answer is exactly the correct minimal answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared log n), using a priority queue (heap).
Space: O(n squared) for the visited array and heap.

blocks.text: Swim in Rising Water is a classic minimax path problem, a variant of Dijkstra's algorithm where the "cost" tracked is a running maximum rather than a running sum.

items: Accumulating elevations as a SUM (like standard Dijkstra) instead of tracking the running MAXIMUM, which would solve a completely different problem.
Forgetting to mark cells visited immediately upon insertion into the priority structure, potentially processing the same cell multiple times.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "this is minimax, not min-sum, so track a running maximum instead of accumulating a total" is the single most important distinction to communicate for this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimize the highest single value encountered along a path", think: a Dijkstra-like priority search tracking a running maximum instead of a running sum.

items: How would you solve this using Union-Find instead, adding cells in increasing order of elevation and checking when top-left and bottom-right first connect?
Path With Minimum Effort, another classic minimax path problem with nearly identical structure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Binary search plus reachability checks costs O(n^2 log(n^2)); the Dijkstra-like priority search costs O(n^2 log n), a slightly more direct single-pass solution.

items: Pattern: minimax path search, a Dijkstra variant tracking a running maximum instead of a running sum.
Core Idea: always expand the lowest-elevation reachable cell next; the running maximum extracted so far is the answer once the destination is reached.
Time: O(n^2 log(n^2)) for the binary search approach, O(n^2 log n) for the priority search.
Most Important Observation: track a running MAXIMUM, not a summed cost, since only the single highest point along a path matters.
Interview Difficulty: a hard, classic minimax-path graph problem.
One line memory trick: Dijkstra, but track the max, not the sum.
